clue.text: Frost report (no rime) in the upper region of Massachusetts

definitions.meaning: a collection by the poet Robert Frost, largely in unrhymed blank verse

definitions.text: in the upper region of Massachusetts

explanation.walkthrough: Robert Frost's 1914 book is mostly blank verse, hence the joke 'no rime' (rhyme, with a frosty pun on rime).
explanation.definitionFit: The title names a stretch of New England lying above Massachusetts's capital city.

clue.text: Enid Bagnold's anti-vet novella reedited

indicators.note: material that is reedited is reworked, so the letters of these words are put in a new order

explanation.surface: An editor has reworked a short novel by Enid Bagnold about an anti-vet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reedited' rearranges ANTIVET plus NOVELLA into the title of Bagnold's famous 1935 horse story.
explanation.definitionFit: The possessive stands for a book written by Bagnold, her best-known horse-racing story.

clue.text: What Cobb does to the French Revolution

definitions.text: What Cobb does to the French Revolution

parts.words: What Cobb does to the French Revolution
parts.note: the historian Richard Cobb wrote a book titled ... to the French Revolution; what he does is respond to it

explanation.definitionFit: Responding to events is the verb at the root of the title of Cobb's book.

clue.text: Injured sheep travels to the Isles of the Blessed

indicators.note: something injured is damaged and bent out of shape, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: travels means rides, as on horseback

explanation.surface: A hurt sheep makes its way to the mythical paradise islands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Injured' shuffles SHEEP only; RIDES (travels) joins it in the pool for the ten letters of the garden nymphs' home.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the garden of these nymphs lay in the far west, often identified with the Isles of the Blessed.

clue.text: He enjoys franchise from Glasgow

parts.note: one granted civic freedom, the franchise or privilege of a city, by Glasgow

explanation.definitionFit: A citizen given the freedom of a city holds its franchise, the privileges of membership.

clue.text: Victim of Hercules shows some of the worth roster had

indicators.note: shows some of means part of the following words is on display inside them

explanation.surface: A slain foe of Hercules appears on a list of worthy men.
explanation.definitionFit: This two-headed dog of Geryon was killed by Hercules during his tenth labour.

clue.text: Sort without English support in Meville's valley

indicators.note: without means the letter for English is removed from the valley's name

parts.note: Typee is Herman Melville's first book, set in a valley of the Marquesas

explanation.surface: Some kind of settler lives unsupported by the English in a South Seas valley from Melville.
explanation.walkthrough: The printed 'Meville's' is a misprint for Melville. 'without' drops one E from TYPEE; 'support' only joins the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A kind or category is a synonym: things of one sort are of one kind.

clue.text: "The the little hussy behaved the prettier she looked" (Adam Bede)

definitions.text: "The the little hussy behaved the prettier she looked" (Adam Bede)

parts.words: "The the little hussy behaved the prettier she looked" (Adam Bede)
parts.note: a quotation from George Eliot's novel with a word missing after the first The; the missing comparative describes worse behaviour

explanation.definitionFit: The gap needs a comparative meaning more badly behaved, pairing with prettier.

clue.text: Synge characters favouring white horses, no doubt

definitions.meaning: a one-act play by J. M. Synge about Aran islanders
white horses are breaking waves, so people keen on them would be heading for the ocean on horseback

explanation.walkthrough: White horses are the foaming crests of waves, a sense the clue plays against real horses.
explanation.definitionFit: The play's title names people on horseback bound for the ocean, which suits those fond of breakers.

clue.text: Friend of Falstaff offers excerpt from book

definitions.meaning: Doll, the prostitute in Shakespeare's Henry IV Part 2
a page torn from a publication

explanation.definitionFit: Doll of that surname is Falstaff's companion, and the common noun is a page removed from a printed volume.

clue.text: Biblical correspondent I find, publishing letters to Niels Bohr

parts.note: Saint Paul wrote the epistles, letters, of the New Testament

explanation.surface: A New Testament letter-writer finds himself writing to a Danish physicist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'find' is a link. The physicist Wolfgang Pauli corresponded at length with Bohr, and the letters were published.
explanation.definitionFit: The Austrian physicist's correspondence with Bohr is a well-known published collection.

clue.text: "A judicious eye instantly rejects anything " (Henry Fielding)

definitions.text: "A judicious eye instantly rejects anything " (Henry Fielding)

parts.words: "A judicious eye instantly rejects anything " (Henry Fielding)
parts.note: a quotation from Tom Jones with its last word missing: something extravagant or exaggerated

explanation.definitionFit: A discerning eye refuses whatever is bizarre or beyond the bounds of propriety.

clue.text: Highly honoured author's indomitable sister and mother in novel form — a rare adventure

definitions.text: Highly honoured author's indomitable sister and mother

indicators.note: in tells us the answer sits inside the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: A Nobel winner's heroine, sister and mother, gets a novel's form in a rare adventure.
explanation.walkthrough: Doris Lessing, a Nobel laureate, wrote Mara and Dann, whose resilient heroine is Dann's sister and later a mother; 'adventure' describes that book.
explanation.definitionFit: Lessing's heroine of that name protects her brother and later bears a child in the sequel.

clue.text: Eleanor Farjeon's court was shaking in it

definitions.text: Eleanor Farjeon's court was shaking in it

parts.words: Eleanor Farjeon's court was shaking in it
parts.note: in Farjeon's Cinderella play The Glass Slipper, the royal court trembles over who will fit the footwear

explanation.definitionFit: The glass slipper is footwear, and the court's suspense centres on it.

clue.text: Little man from Mann

parts.note: Thomas Mann's early story Little Herr ... is about a small hunchbacked man

explanation.definitionFit: The title character of Mann's story is the little man of its name.

clue.text: He kept harping on the wall at Thebes

definitions.text: He kept harping on the wall at Thebes

parts.words: He kept harping on the wall at Thebes
parts.note: in Greek myth, a son of Zeus played his lyre so well that stones moved themselves to form the walls of Thebes

explanation.definitionFit: The mythical lyre player raised Thebes's walls with music, literally harping on about them.

clue.text: Shrewd as Dekker's copper?

definitions.meaning: Thomas Dekker's pamphlet ..., Pound-Foolish; a copper is a penny

explanation.walkthrough: A copper is a British penny coin; Dekker's 1631 pamphlet title begins with the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Being careful over small amounts of money is a kind of thrifty shrewdness.

clue.text: Father of Tolstoy

parts.note: not Tolstoy's parent but the monk who gives his name to Tolstoy's novella Father ...

explanation.definitionFit: Tolstoy's late novella is named after a monk, Father of that name.

clue.text: Father of Alan Paton

parts.note: not Paton's parent but the English priest in Cry, the Beloved Country

explanation.definitionFit: Paton's novel features a priest called Father by that name who helps Kumalo in Johannesburg.

clue.text: Stray tendril exhibited by Walpole's governess

indicators.note: stray means wandering off course, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A wayward plant shoot is displayed by a governess in a Hugh Walpole novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stray' rearranges TENDRIL; 'exhibited by' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Miss of that name is the governess in Hugh Walpole's novel The Golden Scarecrow.

clue.text: First Roosevelt briefly holding symbol of high office used instrumentally

indicators.note: holding means the first piece wraps round the second

parts.note: Theodore Roosevelt was the first President Roosevelt; Theo is his name cut short
an orb is part of the regalia of a monarch

explanation.surface: Teddy Roosevelt grips a sceptre-like emblem of power as a tool.
explanation.definitionFit: This large bass lute was a thing used in playing music, an instrument.

clue.text: Formal tunics of volunteers with poets

parts.note: TA is the Territorial Army, Britain's volunteer reserve force
poets are bards

explanation.surface: Volunteers and poets dress in ceremonial tunics.
explanation.definitionFit: Heralds wear these short ceremonial coats emblazoned with arms.

clue.text: Bets on Macaulay's songs

definitions.meaning: ... of Ancient Rome, Macaulay's narrative poems

explanation.definitionFit: To wager is a sense of the verb, and the noun means ballads, as in Macaulay's title.

clue.text: Sikes identified Oliver as a young one

definitions.text: Sikes identified Oliver as a young one

parts.words: Sikes identified Oliver as a young one
parts.note: in Oliver Twist, Bill Sikes calls the boy a young rascal, using the slang for a mischievous child

explanation.definitionFit: Dickensian slang for a naughty child, the devil's young offshoot.

clue.text: Seen at forest location in Tennyson's work

definitions.text: Seen at forest location in Tennyson's work

parts.words: Seen at forest location in Tennyson's work
parts.note: Tennyson's poem pairs the hero's name with Arden, the forest in As You Like It

explanation.definitionFit: Tennyson's sailor hero is called by this first name and the Arden surname.

clue.text: Bilingual agreement for Louise Ramé

parts.note: oui is French for yes
da is Russian for yes

explanation.surface: A novelist's name is a yes said in two languages.
explanation.definitionFit: This pen name was used by the English novelist born Maria Louise Ramé.

clue.text: Angela, with whom Seal sealed matters

definitions.text: Angela, with whom Seal sealed matters

parts.words: Angela, with whom Seal sealed matters
parts.note: in Evelyn Waugh's Put Out More Flags, Basil Seal has a long affair with Angela

explanation.definitionFit: Waugh's Angela bears this surname as Basil Seal's wealthy mistress.

clue.text: Her "brother's" name was Acton

parts.note: the Brontë sisters published as the Bell brothers; Anne was Acton Bell, sister of the one who was Ellis

explanation.definitionFit: Anne's sister, who wrote as Ellis Bell, had a pseudonymous 'brother' named Acton.

clue.text: Ruins add a twist for a bit part in Julius Caesar

definitions.text: a bit part in Julius Caesar

indicators.note: a twist distorts something, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Damage gives an unexpected turn to a small role in Shakespeare.
explanation.definitionFit: This servant of Brutus has only a few lines in Shakespeare's Roman play.

clue.text: Millworker's predicament exploited by Huxley

definitions.meaning: Milton's blinded Samson laments being sightless in the Philistine city, at the mill with slaves
Aldous Huxley took Milton's phrase as the title of his 1936 novel

explanation.definitionFit: The phrase from Samson Agonistes describes the captive's blindness at the mill, and Huxley borrowed it.
